Logical vs Physical Qubits

Logical vs physical qubits: this distinction is absolutely central to understanding how quantum computers actually work in practice.

The logical qubit behaves as one mathematical unit, but physically it requires hundreds or thousands of synchronized hardware channels, all operating in parallel with nanosecond precision, and continuously corrected by classical feedback loops.

Physical Qubits

The real, hardware-level qubits built in a lab — the physical systems that hold quantum information.

  • Superconducting loops (IBM, Google)
  • Trapped ions (IonQ, Honeywell)
  • Photons (PsiQuantum)
  • Spins in semiconductors (Intel, Delft)

Each physical qubit can be in a quantum superposition of |0⟩ and |1⟩. However, they are noisy — prone to decoherence and operational errors (bit flips, phase flips, crosstalk, etc.). Their coherence time (how long they can maintain a quantum state) is often microseconds to milliseconds. Gates (quantum operations) have limited fidelity (typically 99%–99.9%).

physical qubits = raw, imperfect building blocks.

Logical Qubits

A fault-tolerant, error-corrected qubit that encodes a single unit of logical quantum information across many physical qubits. Purpose is to protect quantum information from noise and errors through quantum error correction (QEC). A single logical qubit might be encoded using 1,000+ physical qubits (for near-term estimates). The surface code is the most common QEC scheme: it arranges qubits on a 2D grid so that local measurements detect and correct errors without destroying the encoded information.

The Ratio Problem

Because error correction is so resource-intensive, if you need 1,000 logical qubits to run a useful algorithm (e.g., factoring or simulating a complex molecule), and each logical qubit needs ~1,000 physical qubits for error correction, you might need a billion physical qubits for a full-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer.

Current machines (as of 2025):

  • IBM Condor → ~1,200 physical qubits
  • IonQ Forte → ~35–40 high-fidelity ion-trap qubits

So we’re still far from even one fully fault-tolerant logical qubit.

Quantum algorithms (Shor’s, Grover’s, QAOA, etc.) assume error-free operations — i.e. logical qubits.
Today’s “NISQ” (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) devices use physical qubits directly, meaning their results are approximate and noise-limited. The future (so-called FTQC — Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing**) will operate entirely on logical qubits, enabling truly scalable and reliable computation.

Aspect Physical Qubit Logical Qubit
Level Hardware Error-corrected abstraction
Error-prone? Yes Designed to be fault-tolerant

Use today NISQ devices Future scalable quantum computers
Typical count per logical qubit 1 1,000–10,000+
Example code – Surface code, Bacon–Shor, color code

how can many physical qbits effectively act as a single one?

This goes to the heart of quantum error correction (QEC) and why logical qubits even exist.

Physical qubits are fragile: they lose quantum information through decoherence (interaction with the environment). Gates and measurements introduce errors (bit-flip, phase-flip, or both). Unlike classical bits, you can’t just copy a qubit’s state to back it up — the no-cloning theorem forbids this.
So, we need another way to protect quantum information without copying it.

Encoding by Entanglement

Instead of one physical qubit storing one logical value, we spread the same quantum information across many entangled qubits. For example:

|0_L⟩ = |000⟩, \quad |1_L⟩ = |111⟩

This is a simplified 3-qubit code. If one qubit flips (say |111⟩ → |101⟩), we can detect and correct it by checking parity relationships between qubits — without measuring their actual quantum state. The logical state (|0_L⟩ or |1_L⟩) is not in any one qubit, but in the global pattern of the group.

Quantum Error Correction Codes (QECC)

There are many such encoding schemes — the most famous being the surface code:

  • Qubits are arranged in a 2D grid.
  • Some are data qubits (hold logical info).
  • Others are ancilla (syndrome) qubits used to check for errors. Each ancilla interacts locally with its neighbours and detects whether an error has occurred — without collapsing the logical state.

The logical qubit is the stable pattern that persists even when some of the underlying qubits fail — as long as errors are sparse and detected in time.

Each physical qubit participates in joint measurements that enforce consistency across the whole code. These measurements tell you where an error likely happened (the “syndrome”). A classical decoder interprets the syndrome and instructs the hardware to correct it.

As long as the error rate per qubit is below a threshold (~1%), and the error correction cycles run fast enough, then the logical qubit’s information remains coherent for a much longer time than any single physical qubit could manage.

Imagine a flock of birds: One bird (physical qubit) might stray off course (error). The flock (logical qubit) maintains direction because the group behavior corrects for small deviations — each bird checks its neighbours. The formation carries the information, not any individual bird.

When we build a “logical qubit,” we’re really creating a self-correcting structure of physical qubits:

  • It can detect and fix small disturbances.
  • It encodes quantum information nonlocally — so local noise can’t easily destroy it.

As you add more physical qubits to the code, the logical qubit’s reliability improves exponentially.

So many qbits are entangled so that they can be read as a single one.

Entanglement as the Glue

When we build a logical qubit, the underlying physical qubits are entangled — meaning their quantum states are linked in such a way that the system as a whole has a well-defined logical state, even though no single qubit does. You can’t point to one qubit and say “that’s the value.” - the entire pattern across them encodes the logical information. This is why the information becomes non-local: it’s distributed, and therefore more robust to local errors.

Encoded Logical States

For a simple example (3-qubit bit-flip code):

|0_L⟩ = |000⟩,\quad |1_L⟩ = |111⟩

But these aren’t just three independent bits — they’re entangled superpositions during real computation, e.g.

|\psi_L⟩ = \alpha|000⟩ + \beta|111⟩

The amplitudes \alpha and \beta belong to the logical qubit. If one qubit flips (say the middle one), the correlations among the three change in a detectable way, but \alpha and \beta remain recoverable after correction.

Error Detection via Correlations

The quantum computer doesn’t directly measure the logical qubit (that would collapse it).
Instead, it measures stabilizers — special parity checks that reveal whether the collective state still matches the expected entangled pattern. These stabilizers tell you where an error happened (a “syndrome”), without revealing the logical information itself. That’s what allows:

  • Detection of errors (bit-flip or phase-flip),
  • Correction using classical decoding logic,
  • Preservation of the logical state across many cycles.

Because all physical qubits participate in enforcing the same global entangled state, any valid operation (logical gate, measurement, etc.) is defined over the entire encoded set - the computer treats that set as a single logical entity. Errors on individual qubits are continuously detected and corrected beneath that abstraction. So many entangled qubits collectively behave as one effective qubit whose coherence time and reliability are vastly improved.

Control hardware

Even though the quantum processor is made of qubits, all the control and correction is handled by classical electronics:

  • Microwave generators (for superconducting qubits),
  • Laser and radio-frequency systems (for trapped ions),
  • fast optical/electronic pulse controllers (for photonic qubits).

Each physical qubit has control lines for applying quantum gates (rotations, entangling operations), initializing (resetting) it, measuring its state, and communicating with its neighbours (for entanglement and stabilizer checks). The control system must address and synchronize many qubits at once.

Parallelism & Timing

In large surface-code grids, hundreds or thousands of qubits are constantly being:

Entangled to enforce stabilizers,
Measured to read error syndromes,
Corrected (based on classical decoding).

All of that happens in tight timing cycles, often every few microseconds. Each cycle might involve:

  • 2-qubit gates on specific pairs (CNOTs or CZs),
  • Single-qubit rotations,
  • Ancilla measurement and reset,
  • Classical decoding and feedback.

To maintain coherence, all these pulses must be phase-synchronized with sub-nanosecond precision.

The Architecture Challenge

This means a fully error-corrected quantum computer has two interlocking machines:

Quantum plane: Physical qubits + couplers Quantum
Control plane: Pulse sequencing, timing, feedback, decoding Classical

And these two layers exchange data continuously:

Quantum → (measurements) → Classical decoder → (correction signals) → Quantum.

That’s why quantum control systems look more like miniature supercomputers sitting right next to a cryostat.

Scalability Issues

As we scale up, each qubit needs 2–4 control lines, so cryogenic wiring and power dissipation become major bottlenecks. Engineers are developing cryogenic CMOS controllers and multiplexed control buses so that many qubits can share the same hardware channels.

For example:

  • Intel’s “Horse Ridge” chip integrates cryogenic control electronics near the qubits.
  • Google’s Sycamore and IBM’s Eagle/Condor processors use complex microwave multiplexing to address many qubits in parallel.

Speed of light

The way the speed of light limits performance is subtle — it’s less about fundamental relativity and more about timing, synchronization, and feedback latency between the quantum and classical control layers.

Quantum Operations Happen Extremely Fast

Quantum gate times:

  • Superconducting qubits: ~10–100 nanoseconds per gate
  • Trapped ions: ~1–100 microseconds
  • Error-correction cycles (surface code): often every microsecond

Each cycle involves:

  1. Running quantum gates,
  2. Measuring ancilla qubits,
  3. Sending measurement data to a classical decoder,
  4. Calculating corrections,
  5. Sending feedback pulses back to qubits.

That’s a round trip between the quantum chip and the classical electronics — and light-speed delay now matters.

Speed of Light = ~30 cm per Nanosecond

That means if your control hardware is 1 meter away, signals take ~3 ns each way. For superconducting qubits, whose operations are tens of nanoseconds long, that’s a significant fraction of a gate time. Hence, every centimeter of wiring adds measurable latency — especially critical in cryogenic systems where signals must travel through temperature stages (10 mK → 300 K), and error correction, which depends on tight, real-time feedback.

Cryogenic Architecture Makes It Worse

Quantum chips sit inside dilution refrigerators at millikelvin temperatures. Classical control electronics (digital logic, FPGAs, GPUs) typically run at room temperature. So, signals must travel:

Quantum plane (10 mK)
↓
Wiring harness
↓
Cryostat feedthroughs
↓
Control electronics (300 K)

This distance might be 1–2 meters of coaxial cable — introducing tens of nanoseconds of latency per direction, plus amplification and conversion delays. That’s why cryogenic control chips (like Intel’s Horse Ridge or IBM’s Cryo-CMOS) are being developed: to push classical control closer to the qubits and reduce these light-speed delays.

Error Correction Latency Is the Bottleneck

In surface-code systems, the decoding step — interpreting measurement results and deciding on corrections — must happen faster than errors accumulate. If the feedback loop is too slow, the logical qubit decoheres. This total latency includes:

  • Signal propagation** (limited by c),
  • Amplifier response time,
  • Analog-to-digital conversion,
  • Classical decoding computation,
  • Return propagation.

So the speed of light sets a hard lower bound on this chain, and engineering aims to approach that limit.

Scaling Implications

If quantum processors grow from 1,000 → 1,000,000 qubits, they’ll physically occupy larger areas: internal signal routing distances grow, and even on-chip propagation (at ~0.3c in superconducting lines) adds up. Future quantum supercomputers may therefore need distributed, modular architectures — separate “quantum tiles” connected by quantum interconnects (photonic or microwave links) with localized control units, to avoid light-speed bottlenecks in long-range wiring.

Mathematical theory

The concept of logical qubits and quantum error correction (QEC) was born first as mathematical theory, not as an experimental discovery. When physicists first began thinking about quantum computing (Feynman, Deutsch, Benioff, 1980s), a key puzzle arose: “If quantum states collapse when measured and can’t be copied, how can we protect information from noise?”

In classical computing, you just duplicate bits and use parity checks. But in quantum mechanics, duplication (copying) is impossible due to the no-cloning theorem (Wootters & Zurek, 1982). So theorists had to invent an entirely new mathematical structure that could preserve information without copying it.

Two papers changed everything:

  • Peter Shor (1995) — “Scheme for reducing decoherence in quantum computer memory”
    → Introduced the first quantum error-correcting code, encoding one logical qubit into 9 physical qubits (the “Shor code”).
  • Andrew Steane (1996) — “Error correcting codes in quantum theory”
    → Simplified Shor’s idea, producing the 7-qubit Steane code based on classical Hamming codes.

These were purely mathematical constructions: Logical states like

|0_L⟩ = (|0000000⟩ + |1111111⟩)/√2

could detect and correct both bit-flip and phase-flip errors. They showed that redundancy via entanglement can protect quantum information. At that time, no hardware could even test them — qubits didn’t yet exist experimentally.

Once basic codes were formalized, theorists proved something astonishing: If each physical qubit and gate has an error rate below a certain threshold, then with enough encoding and correction, you can perform arbitrarily long, accurate quantum computations. This is known as the Quantum Fault-Tolerance Theorem, developed by Shor, Aharonov, Ben-Or, Knill, Laflamme, and others (1996–1998). It was a mathematical proof of possibility: Quantum computation can, in principle, overcome noise — not by luck, but by design.

After the first generation of algebraic codes (Shor, Steane), researchers looked for more efficient and physically realistic ones. Kitaev (2003) proposed the toric code — a geometric, topological error correction scheme. This evolved into the surface code (Raussendorf, Fowler, et al., 2007–2012), which maps logical qubits onto a 2D lattice. Surface codes became the standard because they’re compatible with planar fabrication — what today’s superconducting and ion-trap qubits use.

Only recently (Google, IBM, ETH Zürich, Quantinuum) have experiments begun to demonstrate single logical qubits — using 9, 17, or 49 physical qubits to encode one logical unit with measurable error suppression.

The mathematics came first by about 20 years.

Next steps

Today, the mathematics of quantum error correction and logical qubits is far ahead of what we can yet test. Here’s where the frontier of theory lies — the parts that are still mostly unverified experimentally.

Beyond the Surface Code — Advanced Topological Models

The surface code dominates current experiments, but mathematically it’s just one member of a vast family of topological quantum error-correcting codes. Researchers are exploring Color codes, subsystem codes, LDPC (low-density parity-check) quantum codes — mathematically elegant, with lower overhead than the surface code. Also, Fracton codes and hyperbolic codes, which live in non-Euclidean or higher-dimensional geometries. These could theoretically encode far more logical qubits per physical qubit, reduce correction cycles and offer self-correcting behaviour (no need for constant active correction).

They do however require qubit connectivity or interaction geometries that no current hardware can achieve (e.g., 3D lattices or long-range couplings).

Self-Correcting Quantum Memories

Mathematical physics predicts the possibility of quantum memories that protect themselves through physical symmetries — no active error correction needed.

Examples:

  • 4D toric codes (Kitaev, 2003)
  • Haah’s cubic code (2011)
  • Fracton topological phases (2015+)

These are rigorous mathematical models that show stability of quantum information in principle, much like a ferromagnet retains alignment below its Curie temperature. They do however require four spatial dimensions or exotic Hamiltonians not realizable in current 3D matter, and no known material naturally supports such self-correcting topological order.

Quantum LDPC Codes and Asymptotic Bounds

Classical LDPC codes are near the Shannon limit — highly efficient. Quantum analogues (QLDPC) were long thought impossible until 2020–2022, when new asymptotically good quantum codes were proven to exist mathematically (e.g., Panteleev & Kalachev 2021). These codes could, in theory achieve constant overhead (not thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit) and enable scalable quantum computation with realistic error rates. No hardware can yet implement these large, complex parity-check networks; all current systems still rely on small, local patches.

Fault-Tolerant Gate Constructions

Mathematically, universal quantum computation requires non-Clifford gates (like the T gate). You can’t directly protect these gates with standard error correction — so theorists invented magic state distillation and lattice surgery. Now, ongoing theory pushes toward:

  • Transversal gates that avoid distillation entirely.
  • Constant-depth fault-tolerant circuits (Haah, Bravyi, Campbell, etc.).
  • Subsystem symmetry-protected computation.

We can’t yet implement large-scale logical circuits or measure how these complex gate protocols behave under real noise models.

Mathematics of Noise and Decoherence — Beyond Stochastic Models

Most quantum error correction assumes errors are random and independent. But in real hardware, noise is often correlated (cross-talk, drift, leakage). New mathematics explores Non-Markovian noise (memory effects), Hamiltonian noise models and error mitigation strategies that operate in analog regimes rather than discrete correction cycles. Experimental noise is difficult to model exactly; only small systems can be fully characterized.

Quantum Gravity & Holography Links

Here’s where mathematics gets profoundly abstract but very exciting:

  • The AdS/CFT correspondence and holographic principle suggest that spacetime geometry itself behaves like a quantum error-correcting code.
  • Tensor network models (e.g., HaPPY code) describe black hole information preservation using QEC mathematics.

So, in theoretical physics, Quantum error correction is no longer just a computing tool — it’s a candidate *mechanism for how the universe encodes information. This operates at the intersection of quantum gravity and information theory — completely outside experimental reach (for now).

The frontier of mathematics is designing ever more elegant, efficient, and physically plausible ways to encode quantum information. The frontier of engineering is catching up — trying to realize even one of those ideas in real hardware.
